190.title: The caliph finds him
190.hook: Caliph Umar, sent by a dream, brings him gold, and the harper weeps at being seen (Masnavi 1)
190.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, stories like this one are read as a picture of God noticing the forgotten, and many readers take it as a reason to look for the people others pass by.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old harper walked out to the graveyard and played for God alone. Your line was play for no one. What did you do with no audience? Day one hundred ninety.

You probably know the feeling of being noticed when you thought nobody was looking. The teacher who stopped you in the hall to say she'd read what you wrote. The boss who remembered the thing you did quietly months ago. A stranger who saw you were struggling and just asked. It can undo you. You can hold it together for years, and one person seeing you is what makes you cry. We left the old harper asleep on a grave, his harp for a pillow. Somebody is on the way. Today: the caliph finds him.
screen: `NOTICED WHEN NOBODY WAS LOOKING.` → `ASLEEP ON A GRAVE.` → `THE CALIPH FINDS HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's how Rumi goes on. While the harper sleeps, the caliph Umar also falls asleep, and a voice comes to him in a dream. It tells him that a servant of God is lying in the graveyard, and that he should take seven hundred gold dinars from the treasury and bring them to him. Umar gets up and goes. He walks the whole graveyard. He sees nobody but an old man asleep, and thinks, surely not him. He circles again. Still only the old man. And then it dawns on him: this is the one. Picture it. The most powerful man in the city is standing over a worn-out musician, the kind of man pious people might pass without a glance. Umar waits by him until he stirs. The harper opens his eyes, sees the caliph, and starts to shake. He assumes he's in trouble. Umar tells him not to be afraid. He has come with good news. God sends greetings, and this gold, and there's more when it runs out. That's when the harper breaks. He weeps, and in Rumi's telling he flings his harp down and smashes it, crying out that it had stood between him and God. He mourns all the years he'd spent performing. The gold barely matters. What undoes him is that he was seen. Sufi readers take the heart of the story to be this: the one nobody wanted, playing to empty graves, had an audience after all. Your line: you were seen.
screen: `A DREAM, AND SEVEN HUNDRED DINARS.` · `SURELY NOT HIM.` · `THE HARPER SHAKES, THEN WEEPS.` · then, large: `YOU WERE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see someone overlooked. Settle, and let someone come to mind who gets passed by. The person who cleans the building, the quiet cousin, the neighbor who lives alone, an older relative who doesn't get many calls. Hold them in mind for a while, with no plan. Just see them, the way Umar finally saw the old man on the grave. If you pray, you can hold them there too. The bell holds the time.
The caliph finds him. Sent by a dream, Umar searches a graveyard, finds only the old harper, and brings him gold and greetings from God. Today's word.
Your line: you were seen. Today, let the person you thought of know it: a message, a thank-you, or just saying their name and meaning it. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Past the veil
191.hook: the harper is told even his regret about the past is a veil to move beyond (Masnavi 1)
191.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, repentance matters, but teachers often warn against getting stuck in regret; the goal described in stories like this is fana, a passing away of the self-centered self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the caliph found the old harper in the graveyard, and he wept at being noticed. Your line was you were seen. Who did you see? Day one hundred ninety-one.

Some people apologize for the same thing for twenty years. The friend who still brings up how she behaved at her sister's wedding. The dad who can't stop saying he worked too much when the kids were small. The regret is real, and it was once useful. But at some point the regret itself becomes the thing they carry around, heavier than whatever happened. We left the old harper on the grave, weeping over his whole life. The caliph is about to say something surprising about those tears. Today: past the veil.
screen: `THE SAME APOLOGY FOR TWENTY YEARS.` → `THE HARPER, WEEPING.` → `PAST THE VEIL.`

segments.voice: The harper is mourning his seventy years of music, the harp he just smashed, all the breath he spent on other people. You'd expect Umar to praise him. Finally, real repentance. Instead, in Rumi's telling, Umar says: this weeping of yours is also a sign that you're still awake to yourself. Your eyes are still on the past. And the past, and the future, are veils between you and God. Burn them both. How long will you stay tied up in these knots? A veil, in Rumi's language, is anything that hangs between you and what's real. Your pride can be a veil. So can your shame. The harper had moved from one to the other: first he was proud of his voice, now he's sorry about it. Either way, the story is still about him. Umar invites him one step further, past both. Rumi says the harper's heart woke up. He stopped weeping, and he stopped laughing too. He went into a state Rumi says can't be described, and the poem simply lets him go. Sufis call this passing away of the small self fana. You don't need that word to feel the point. There comes a time when even your regrets are just more ways of staring at yourself. Rumi isn't saying the past doesn't matter. He's saying you can't live facing backward. And that brings our week together. The parrot that played dead to get free. Marcus's inner retreat. Change as nature's favorite thing. An old man who played for no one, was seen, and walked past the veil. Your line: past the veil.
screen: `EVEN YOUR TEARS ARE STILL ABOUT YOU.` · `PAST AND FUTURE ARE VEILS.` · `NO WEEPING, NO LAUGHING.` · then, large: `PAST THE VEIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one self-judgment. Settle, and find one thing you keep holding against yourself. Something old, not something that still needs fixing. Look at it plainly for a breath or two. Then imagine setting it down beside you, the way the harper finally put his weeping down. You're not pretending it didn't happen. You're just not carrying it for the next two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Past the veil. Umar tells the weeping harper that even his regret is a veil, and he moves beyond it into a state Rumi won't describe. Today's word.
Your line: past the veil. Today, when the old judgment comes back, notice it, say the line, and leave it where you set it down. Day one hundred ninety-one.

192.title: Like the vine
192.hook: a vine gives grapes and asks nothing more, so do good and move on (Meditations 5.6)
192.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this passage as a check on their own motives, and many traditions share a version of the idea that good done quietly, without keeping score, is good done well.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the old harper walking past even his own regret. Your line was past the veil. Did the old judgment come back, and did you leave it where you set it down? Day one hundred ninety-two.

You hold the door for someone and they don't say thanks. And there it is: a tiny flash of annoyance. Or you help a friend move, carry the couch down three flights, and a month later you're still keeping score, just a little. Most of us do good things and then hang around the good thing, waiting for it to be noticed. A new week starts today, and it's called the shepherd, for a story coming in two days. But first, Marcus has a picture for that little scorekeeper in us. It grows on a trellis. Today: like the vine.
screen: `NO THANKS FOR THE DOOR.` → `STILL KEEPING SCORE.` → `LIKE THE VINE.`

segments.voice: In Book Five of the Meditations, Marcus sorts people who do good into three kinds. The first does you a favor and is ready to send the bill: you owe me. The second doesn't ask for anything out loud, but quietly thinks of you as someone in their debt, and knows exactly what they did. And the third, Marcus says, in a way doesn't even know what he has done. He's like a vine that has produced grapes and asks for nothing more once it has borne its own fruit. Then Marcus piles up more pictures. A horse that has run its race. A dog that has tracked the game. A bee that has made its honey. None of them calls everyone over to look. They just go on to the next thing, the way the vine, next season, simply makes grapes again. That's what doing good looks like when it's part of your nature, not a transaction. Marcus imagines someone objecting: surely a decent person should notice what they've done? He grants the point, then warns that this is how you slide back into the first kind of person. The vine isn't being humble. Being humble would still be about the vine. It's just being a vine. Giving grapes is what vines do. For Marcus, being helpful is what a human being is for, so helping isn't a favor you've done anyone. It's you working properly. And the reward is already in it, the way the grapes are already the vine's whole point. Your line: like the vine.
screen: `THREE KINDS OF PEOPLE WHO DO GOOD.` · `A VINE THAT ASKS NOTHING MORE.` · `THE HORSE, THE DOG, THE BEE.` · then, large: `LIKE THE VINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help once and don't mention it. For now, sit and think of one small thing you could do for someone today. Refill something, fix something, send something, take a chore off someone's list. Picture yourself doing it, and then picture yourself walking away without saying a word. Notice what part of you wants credit. Let it be there, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Like the vine. Marcus says the best kind of good is like a vine that gives its grapes and asks for nothing more, then does it again next season. Today's word.
Your line: like the vine. Today, do the thing you pictured, and don't mention it to anyone, not even in passing. Day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: The mind is dyed
193.hook: your mind takes the color of the thoughts you keep (Meditations 5.16)
193.howItsDone: Many readers of the Stoics keep a few short lines to return to through the day, and some write them on cards or repeat them at set times, the way Marcus repeated his own reminders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus's vine gave its grapes and asked for nothing. Your line was like the vine. Did you manage to help without mentioning it? Day one hundred ninety-three.

Drop a white T-shirt into a pot of hot water with one red sock. It doesn't take much, and it doesn't take long. Everything comes out pink. Now think about the thoughts that go round in your head on a normal day. The comment someone made at work. The worry about money. The replay of an argument you already lost. Or the song you love, the kid's joke, the thing you're grateful for. You don't choose every thought that shows up. But some of them you keep in the water, over and over. Marcus noticed what that does. Today: the mind is dyed.
screen: `ONE RED SOCK.` → `THE THOUGHTS YOU KEEP IN THE WATER.` → `THE MIND IS DYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the line from Book Five, in George Long's translation: "Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts." The Greek verb Marcus uses is the word for dipping cloth into dye. In his world, dyeing wasn't a quick rinse. You soaked the wool, again and again, until the color went all the way through and wouldn't wash out. That's his picture of a mind. It isn't what you think once that shapes you. It's what you think habitually, the thoughts you dip into every day. So Marcus tells himself to dye his soul on purpose, with a steady run of good thoughts. And he gives an example. Where a person can live, he says, they can also live well. Then he tests it on himself. Someone might say, but I have to live in a palace. Fine, he answers: a person can live well in a palace, too. Remember who's writing. The palace was his actual address. He isn't dreaming of a quiet cabin. He's telling himself that the life he's stuck with can still be lived well, because the color of it comes from inside. Psychologists today talk about rumination, the way a thought on repeat can deepen a low mood. Marcus got there with a dye pot. You can't stop every thought from coming. You can choose which ones you keep dipping into. Your line: dyed by thoughts.
screen: `THE SOUL IS DYED BY THE THOUGHTS.` · `DIPPED AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `YOU CAN LIVE WELL IN A PALACE, TOO.` · then, large: `DYED BY THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thought to repeat today. Settle, and let a few of your usual thoughts go by. Notice which ones come back most. Then choose one you'd like to soak in instead. Something true and steadying, like: I can live well even here. Or: this day is enough. Or a line from a text you love. Say it slowly inside, a few times, and let it sink in. The bell holds the time.
The mind is dyed. Marcus says your mind takes on the color of the thoughts you keep coming back to. Today's word.
Your line: dyed by thoughts. Today, carry the thought you chose, and repeat it three times: in the morning, at midday and before you sleep. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Moses and the shepherd
194.hook: a shepherd prays to comb God's hair and wash God's feet, and Moses scolds him (Masnavi 2.1720ff)
194.howItsDone: Alongside set prayers, many traditions make room for personal prayer in a person's own words, and readers of Rumi often point to this story when they talk about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said the soul is dyed by the thoughts it keeps. Your line was dyed by thoughts. What thought did you soak in? Day one hundred ninety-four.

Listen to a small child pray at bedtime. Thank you for the dog. Please make Grandma's knee better. Are you cold up there? Adults sometimes smile, and sometimes wince a little: that's not how you talk to God. There's a right way, isn't there? The proper words, the ones in the book. Rumi tells a story about exactly this, and it is one of the most loved stories in the whole Masnavi. It's the story this week is named for, and it takes three days. It begins with a man alone on a hillside with his goats. Today: Moses and the shepherd.
screen: `ARE YOU COLD UP THERE?` → `THE PROPER WORDS.` → `MOSES AND THE SHEPHERD.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Two. Moses, the great prophet whom Jews, Christians and Muslims all honor, is walking along a road when he hears a shepherd praying out loud. And the prayer goes something like this. God, where are you? Let me be your servant. I'd mend your shoes and comb your hair. I'd wash your clothes and pick out your lice. I'd bring you milk. I'd kiss your little hand and rub your little feet, and sweep out the place where you sleep at night. All my goats are yours. Picture this man. He has no learning. He's offering God the only things he knows how to give: the care you'd give someone you love who's tired and far from home. Moses stops. Who are you talking to? The shepherd says: the one who made us, and made the earth and sky. And Moses is horrified. In Rumi's telling, he tells the shepherd he's talking nonsense, that he should stuff cotton in his mouth, that God has no need of shoes and socks and milk. Talk like that, Moses says, is fit for a body that grows and needs feeding, not for God. Now, Moses isn't wrong about God. Rumi's tradition, like many, teaches that God has no body. But watch what the scolding does. The shepherd says, you've shut my mouth and set my soul on fire with regret. He tears his clothes, lets out a long sigh, turns, and walks away into the desert. Tomorrow we find out what God thinks. Today, just notice the prayer itself, clumsy and completely sincere. Your line: in your own words.
screen: `A SHEPHERD PRAYS OUT LOUD.` · `I'D COMB YOUR HAIR AND WASH YOUR FEET.` · `MOSES: GOD NEEDS NO SHOES.` · then, large: `IN YOUR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks in plain words. Settle, and let one or two things come to mind that you're grateful for today. Then say thank you for them, inside, in the plainest words you've got. No borrowed phrases, nothing you'd put in a card. Thanks for the coffee. Thanks that the test came back fine. If you pray, you can say it to God. If not, just say it into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Moses and the shepherd. A shepherd prays to comb God's hair and wash God's feet, and the prophet Moses scolds him for it. Today's word.
Your line: in your own words. Today, the next time you feel grateful, say it out loud in your own words, to a person, to God, or to the air. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: Moses is rebuked
195.hook: a voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them (Masnavi 2)
195.howItsDone: Readers of Rumi often cite this story when they talk about respecting other people's ways of prayer, and many Sufi teachers use it to warn against judging sincerity by vocabulary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses scolded a shepherd for offering to comb God's hair, and the shepherd walked off into the desert. Your line was in your own words. Did you say thanks plainly? Day one hundred ninety-five.

Maybe you've been corrected at a moment you were trying your hardest. You cooked for someone and they told you how their mother makes it. You finally opened up about something and got a lecture back. The correction might even have been right. But something closed, and it didn't open again for a long time. Yesterday a shepherd poured out his heart, got corrected by a prophet, and left. Moses, presumably, walked on feeling he'd done his job. Then he hears a voice, and it isn't pleased with him. Today: Moses is rebuked.
screen: `CORRECTED WHILE TRYING YOUR HARDEST.` → `SOMETHING CLOSED.` → `MOSES IS REBUKED.`

segments.voice: In Rumi's telling, a revelation comes to Moses from God, and it goes something like this. You have parted my servant from me. Did you come as a prophet to bring people together, or to split them apart? Rumi puts it in a pair of rhyming lines that Persian speakers still quote: you came to unite, not to sever. Then the voice goes on. I have given every person a way of their own, a way of speaking. What is praise from him would be blame from you. What's honey for one is poison for another. And then Rumi's most famous twist. The voice says: I don't look at the tongue and the words. I look at the heart and its state. Rumi gives an example from his own world: the idiom of India is praise for the people of India, the idiom of Sind for the people of Sind. Different words, the same longing. Notice what the story doesn't say. It doesn't say Moses was wrong that God has no body. Rumi's tradition keeps that teaching. It says Moses was wrong to make the shepherd's words the test of his heart. The man's language was mistaken. His love was not. That's hard for anyone who loves getting things right, and most religious people do, in every tradition. The story isn't against correct teaching. It's a warning about what correction can cost when it lands on someone who is only trying to love. So when you hear someone pray or talk about the sacred in a way that isn't yours, the story suggests a first thought: their words, not mine. Your line.
screen: `YOU HAVE PARTED MY SERVANT FROM ME.` · `YOU CAME TO UNITE, NOT TO SEVER.` · `I LOOK AT THE HEART, NOT THE TONGUE.` · then, large: `THEIR WORDS, NOT MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone's way of praying. Settle, and bring to mind someone whose way with the sacred is different from yours. A grandmother with her beads, a friend who talks to the universe, a colleague who fasts, a child at bedtime. Picture them in the middle of it. Don't correct anything, even inside. Just listen for the heart underneath the words. The bell holds the time.
Moses is rebuked. A voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them, and that God looks at the heart, not the tongue. Today's word.
Your line: their words, not mine. Today, when you hear something said about God or meaning that isn't how you'd say it, think the line before you think anything else. Day one hundred ninety-five.

196.title: Beyond words
196.hook: Moses runs after the shepherd, who has gone past speech altogether (Masnavi 2)
196.howItsDone: Many traditions keep a practice of silent prayer or contemplation alongside spoken prayer, and Rumi, who so often ended his poems by telling himself to be silent, is one of its best-known voices.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses is rebuked: God told him he was sent to unite, not to sever. Your line was their words, not mine. Whose words did you hear differently? Day one hundred ninety-six.

You've maybe run after someone to apologize. Out the door, down the street, heart going, rehearsing what you'll say. And sometimes, when you catch up, you find they've already moved on. Not in anger. They've just gone somewhere you can't quite follow anymore. That's where our story ends. Moses has been rebuked. He knows he has to find the shepherd and set things right. So the prophet goes out into the desert, running. Today, the last part of the story: beyond words.
screen: `RUNNING AFTER SOMEONE TO APOLOGIZE.` → `INTO THE DESERT.` → `BEYOND WORDS.`

segments.voice: Rumi gives us a lovely detail. Moses follows the shepherd's footprints in the sand, and they're all over the place. The steps of someone lost in his own heart: one like a castle on a chessboard, going straight, another like a bishop, going sideways. Finally Moses catches up. And he brings good news. You have permission, he says. Don't look for rules or proper forms. Say whatever your heart wants to say. Your way of praying is the light of faith. Imagine the shepherd hearing that. Except that isn't what happens next. The shepherd answers: Moses, I've gone past that now. I'm soaked in my heart's blood. In Rumi's telling he says he has passed beyond the Lote Tree, the tree that in Islamic tradition marks the farthest boundary of heaven. You struck my horse with your whip, he tells Moses, and it leapt and went beyond the sky. And then he says the most important thing. My state now is beyond telling. What I'm saying to you isn't my state. The scolding didn't just hurt him. It pushed him past the need for words altogether. Rumi then turns to the reader. Whatever you say in praise of God, he says, is like the image a mirror shows. The picture is yours, not the mirror's. Our words about the sacred, all of them, are never the sacred itself. Even the proper ones. Even Moses's. Yesterday was about not judging someone's words. Today goes one step further: at the deepest point, maybe no words fit. Your line: beyond words.
